A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentResponses.content:
# Building DTC Under a 55% Retail Concentration

## Framing: What the Angry Phone Call Actually Told You

**1. The call was about *surprise* and *price*, not about presence.** No buyer at a major retailer believes they can stop a brand from having a website in the 2020s. What they punish is (a) being made to look expensive to their own shoppers, (b) discovering something from a competitor, a price-scraping bot, or their own boss rather than from you, and (c) losing face internally at the moment they were defending your line in an assortment review. Before you design anything, establish which of those three you tripped. The remedies are entirely different, and only one of them ("we were cheaper on a SKU they stock") requires you to change your strategy rather than your process.

**2. "Higher margins" is largely a myth below roughly $40–60M of DTC revenue.** The seductive arithmetic — 50% gross margin at wholesale becomes 75% at retail price — evaporates once you load in paid acquisition, fulfillment of single units to residential addresses, 8–20% return rates, payments, customer service, platform and martech stack, and the fully-loaded team. Most consumer goods companies discover their DTC contribution margin is *below* their retail contribution margin for the first two to three years, and only crosses over when repeat purchase and accessory/consumable attach carry the mix. **Build DTC for data, product incubation, and negotiating leverage. If you build it for margin, you will be tempted to price competitively to drive volume, and that is exactly the move that starts the war.**

**3. Concentration is your real problem; channel conflict is the constraint you solve it under.** 55% in two accounts means a single delisting or a 30% facings reduction is an existential event. That is a structural fragility DTC alone cannot fix — a realistic DTC business is 15–20% of revenue in five years, not 50%. So the honest goal is *diversification of dependence* through multiple vectors (DTC, third and fourth retail partners, marketplace, international, B2B/commercial, subscription) with DTC as the highest-strategic-value but not highest-volume leg. Framing DTC as "the answer to concentration" sets it an impossible task and justifies reckless speed.

**4. You do not need a transactional store to get most of the first-party data.** Roughly 60–70% of the addressable data value — identity, household, product owned, purchase date, usage, satisfaction, replacement timing, consumable cadence — is obtainable through registration, warranty activation, app, content, consumables and service, none of which competes with the retailer for the transaction. **Sequence data ahead of commerce.** This is the single most underused move available to you: you can build a 500,000-record consented first-party database that your partners will actively help you populate, because it costs them nothing.

**5. Your best allies inside those retailers are not the people who called you.** The buying team's incentive is unit economics on their shelf. But the same retailer has a dropship/marketplace team measured on assortment breadth, a retail media team measured on ad revenue from you, and a category director measured on total category growth — all of whom benefit from things the buyer instinctively resists. **Multi-threading the account is not a communication tactic; it is the core of the strategy.** A brand that spends meaningfully in a retailer's media network and supplies their dropship program is structurally much harder to punish.

---

## Phase 0: The 90-Day Diagnostic

**1. Forensic post-mortem on the pilot.** Reconstruct precisely: which SKUs were listed, at what price versus shelf and versus MAP, how the buyer found out, what they threatened, and — critically — **what actually happened afterward**. Did POs drop? Facings shrink? Promotional support get pulled? Or was the anger theater timed to a negotiation? Retailers routinely manufacture outrage to extract terms. If nothing measurable changed, you learned that their bark exceeds their bite, which materially expands your option set.

**2. Partner power audit.** For each of the top two: your share of their category, your margin dollars per linear foot and per square foot versus category average, your sell-through velocity, return rate, attach revenue, and — the most important number — **who else could fill your facings at your velocity and their margin rate**. If the answer is "nobody, quickly," your leverage is far greater than a 55% concentration figure implies. Concentration cuts both ways and incumbents habitually read only their own side of it.

**3. Honest dual-channel P&L.** Build fully-loaded contribution per unit for retail versus a modeled DTC at three scale points ($10M, $30M, $75M). Include CAC by cohort, fulfillment, returns, and reverse logistics. Determine the revenue level at which DTC contribution actually exceeds wholesale contribution. That number governs your investment pacing and prevents the board from expecting margin accretion in year one.

**4. Cannibalization test, quietly and legitimately.** Run a geo-holdout or an existing-owner-only test on non-competing assortment (accessories, consumables, refurbished, DTC-exclusive bundles). Measure whether retail POS in those geos moves at all. In most consumer categories, DTC on non-overlapping assortment is 70–90% incremental. You need this number because it is the central factual claim in every partner conversation you will have for the next three years.

**5. Price and MAP baseline.** Map every SKU's street price across all channels, including marketplace third-party sellers and unauthorized resellers, over 12 months. You will almost certainly find that *your partners' own price violations and marketplace grey sellers* are eroding your price architecture far more than your pilot did. This is the fact that converts your MAP policy from a concession you make into a gift you offer.

---

## The Strategic Verdict

**Build DTC as a data, service, and innovation channel that is structurally never cheaper and never assortment-identical. Sequence data before commerce. Buy every step of channel expansion with a paired, contractual benefit to the partner. And use the three years of peace this purchases to reduce concentration through channels the partners don't police.**

The organizing principle, published internally and stated verbatim to partners:

> **We will never be the cheapest place to buy our products, and we will never compete for the transaction the retailer earned. We will own the relationship with the owner, the second purchase, and the products the shelf cannot carry.**

This is unusually powerful because it is *verifiable*. A partner can check it with a bot every night. A promise a partner can audit is worth ten promises they must trust.

### What we are explicitly *not* doing

- **Not launching a full-line web store.** Not in year one, probably not ever in the form management currently imagines.
- **Not discounting DTC.** No DTC price below shelf on any comparable item, ever, including promotions. Value is delivered in non-price currency (see §2).
- **Not building DTC to be margin-accretive in year one or two.** We will fund it as a capability investment with a defined crossover point and defend that framing to the board explicitly.
- **Not going quiet.** The pilot failed because it was quiet. Stealth converts a manageable negotiation into a betrayal narrative, and betrayal narratives are what get lines delisted.
- **Not treating the two partners identically.** They have different strategies, different e-commerce maturity, and different tolerance. One will likely become a partner in this; the other will need to be managed. Segment them.

---

## 1. Channel Architecture: Four Channels With Four Different Jobs

The failure mode is a channel *lineup* (places to buy the same things) instead of a channel *portfolio* (places that do different jobs). Assign jobs explicitly:

| Channel | Job | Assortment | Owns |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retail partners** (top 2 + others) | Reach, discovery, trial, volume, price anchoring | Hero SKUs, giftable formats, retailer-exclusive derivatives | ~75–80% of units, indefinitely |
| **Brand.com** | Owner relationship, second purchase, service, incubation | Consumables/parts, accessories, refurbished, made-to-order/personalized, DTC-exclusive tiers, bundles, subscriptions, service plans | First-party data, LTV |
| **Retailer dropship / retailer marketplace** | Assortment breadth *inside* the partner, without shelf space | Long-tail sizes, colorways, slower SKUs, seasonal | Extends the partner rather than bypassing them |
| **Marketplace (Amazon et al.)** | Search-intent capture, brand-store control, grey-seller suppression | Curated subset, distinct model numbers where possible | Governance of the digital shelf |

Two architectural choices deserve emphasis:

**Brand.com opens as a "retailer-first" storefront, not a store.** For every hero SKU, the product page ends in a "Where to Buy" module that routes the shopper to the partner — with real-time inventory, store locator, and a click-through the partner can measure. You then *report that traffic to them monthly*. This is a genuine gift: you are converting your brand's organic and paid search demand into their transactions, attributable. It also gives you the single most useful negotiating instrument you will ever have — **the ability to show a buyer exactly how many qualified shoppers you sent them, and to imply, without ever saying it, that this is a choice.**

**Retailer dropship is the most underrated peace-making move available.** It gives you DTC-like unit economics and shipment-level data on assortment the partner would never give shelf space to, while the transaction, the customer, and the credit remain theirs. Buyers approve it enthusiastically because it grows their sales without inventory risk. Lead with this in your first conversation; it makes you a collaborator before you are a competitor.

---

## 2. Product and Pricing Differentiation: Six Inviolable Rules

Differentiation must be *structural* — rooted in what each channel is actually good at — not cosmetic. A different colorway on the same chassis fools nobody and insults the buyer.

**The six rules, written down and shared with partners:**

1. **No shared SKU is ever cheaper on brand.com.** Same model number, same or higher price, including all promotions, always. Audit daily; publish compliance quarterly.
2. **DTC-exclusive products carry distinct model numbers and are differentiated by at least two of:** content/configuration, personalization, bundle composition, service wrap, or format not viable on a shelf (e.g., subscription-sized consumables, multi-packs, made-to-order).
3. **DTC price per comparable unit of value is at or above shelf.** DTC exclusives are positioned *up*, not down — premium tier, personalized, bundled with service. The DTC channel is the price ceiling of the brand, which is a benefit to the retailer's own margin defense.
4. **The retailer gets first-window exclusivity on new hero launches** (typically 60–120 days) before brand.com lists even a "where to buy" page. Newness is the currency buyers care most about; spending it deliberately buys enormous goodwill.
5. **Promotional calendars are shared and synchronized.** Brand.com never promotes into a partner's event window, never front-runs it, and never runs a deeper offer than the partner is running that week.
6. **Consumables, parts, and refurbished are offered to partners first.** If they decline (and on parts they usually will, because the SKU count is uneconomic for shelf), the decline is documented and brand.com carries it. "We offered, you passed" is an unassailable position.

**How DTC delivers value without price.** This is the mechanism that makes the whole plan work. DTC shoppers get things a price-comparison bot cannot see and a retailer cannot easily object to:

- Extended warranty registration (2 years → 5 years) at no charge
- Membership: loyalty credits toward the next purchase, priority service, replenishment discounts on *consumables only*
- Personalization, monogramming, configuration, colorway choice
- Trade-in / take-back credit
- Faster or free shipping, easier returns, direct-to-human service
- Bundles whose *component sum* exceeds the bundle price but where no component is individually cheaper

Note the elegance of the consumables discount: subscription pricing on refills is normal commercial practice, does not touch the hardware price anchor, and generates the recurring relationship that actually makes DTC profitable.

**The incubation offer — the strategic centerpiece.** Position brand.com as the company's product laboratory: new concepts launch DTC at low volume, generate real demand and review data in 90 days, and **graduate the winners to retail with a proven sell-through rate**. This reframes DTC from a threat to a service: you are de-risking the buyer's assortment decisions with your own capital. Formalize it — a quarterly "DTC Signal Report" to each partner showing what tested well, with right of first refusal on the winners. Buyers are evaluated on assortment bets that work. You are offering to make those bets safer. This single mechanism has converted more hostile buyers than any amount of margin concession.

---

## 3. Data Strategy: Climb the Ladder in Order

**The data ladder — each rung requires no permission from the retailer and each one funds the next:**

| Rung | Mechanism | Data captured | Realistic reach |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Registration | Warranty extension for registering, QR in-box, retailer-agnostic | Identity, household, product, purchase date, retailer of purchase | 25–40% of units with strong incentive |
| 2. Engagement | App, content, how-to, community, recipe/usage library | Usage frequency, intent signals, satisfaction | 30–50% of registrants |
| 3. Service | Support tickets, parts orders, out-of-warranty repair | Failure modes, replacement timing | 10–20% of base |
| 4. Consumables/replenishment | Subscription, auto-ship | Purchase cadence, direct revenue, LTV | 5–15% of base initially |
| 5. Transaction | DTC-exclusive and full-line purchase | Full commerce data, CAC/LTV economics | The endpoint, not the start |

**Push hard on rung 1 immediately, before any commerce expansion.** The in-box registration card with a real incentive (three extra years of warranty is worth more to the consumer than it costs you, and it reinforces the durability story) is the highest-ROI investment in this entire plan. It is invisible to the retailer, it generates no conflict, and it can plausibly build a 300,000–600,000 record consented database in 18 months. **You can be data-rich long before you are commerce-rich, and the data is what management actually said it wanted.**

**Make the data a shared asset, not a stolen one.** Three moves:

- **Clean-room collaboration.** Match your first-party registration data against the partner's loyalty data in a privacy-safe clean room to produce joint insight neither of you has alone: who buys your category, what they buy alongside, what the true repeat cycle is, which of their stores under-index versus their own shopper base. Hand them the analysis. A brand that makes the buyer smarter in front of their own leadership becomes very hard to delist.
- **Buy their retail media, meaningfully.** Shift trade dollars into their media network. It funds their highest-margin P&L line, it makes you a customer of a second team inside the account, and it earns you closed-loop measurement data. This is the cheapest political insurance available.
- **Publish a data covenant.** Written commitments: we will not use registration data to solicit a shelf purchase away from the retailer who made it; we will not retarget in-store shoppers with DTC hero-SKU offers; we
